newsitem.title: GERMANY: D. Telekom shares withstand Waigel heat.
newsitem.headline: D. Telekom shares withstand Waigel heat.

text.p: Deutche Telekom AG shares withstood the heat of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday announcing a potential early sale of Bonn's remaining stake in the telephone monopoly as traders viewed Telekom's brief but sharp drop as a nifty buying opportunity.

Shares in Telekom, a DAX index heavyweight, tumbled 1.79 marks to 38.01 marks, or a loss of 4.5 percent, after Waigel said it was conceivable that parts of the privatisation of Bonn's 74 percent stake in Telekom could be brought forward.

But bargain-hunters emerged as concrete details about any share offer, namely that it must be a private placement with Telekom board approval, were announced and Telekom shares recovered to end bourse trade down 93 pfennigs at 39.20 marks.
"People have had some second thoughts and now believe the market has overreacted," said Josh Waiblinger, an assistant vice president of equity sales at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
"The drop should provide an opportunity to buy the shares," he said. "Anything under 40 marks appears to be good value."

Waigel's statement about a potential sale of more Telekom shares could not have come at a worse time since investors who bought Telekom shares in the initial share offering last November will be free from next Monday to sell them without the penalty of hefty German capital-gains taxes.
"It's rather lousy timing from Waigel," a trader said.

The threat of new public shares diluting the value of existing shares may prompt some private investors to dump Telekom, which was offered at 28.50 marks, despite lucrative dividend payouts and a 10 percent bonus share offer for initial shareholders who hold onto the shares for three years.
Traders said they expect Bonn to offer about 10 billion to 15 billion marks in Telekom shares to institutional investors with a long-term view on the telephone group.
"Some private investors may have thought about taking profits despite the warnings of some analysts to hold onto the stock after this episode," said one Frankfurt share trader.

"But I think it's a good time to buy Telekom at these levels," the analyst said. "There are still a number of institutional investors who are underweighted on Telekom and that will certainly support the share at these levels."
Still, some traders said U.S. institutional investors were disappointed by Waigel's statement and were a factor in selling pressure during morning pre-bourse IBIS computer dealings.
They were particularly upset at Waigel seeking to use the proceeds to plug Bonn's budget debt in a bid to whip Germany's finances into shape for European currency union, traders said.

Telekom Chairman Ron Sommer, seeking to play down the uproar caused by Waigel, told the daily Bild newspaper in a report to be published on Thursday that German law requires Bonn to seek approval from Telekom for a sale of shares that would impact the public share market before December 31, 1999.
"We will ensure that the interests of the nearly two million shareholders are not affected. There is complete agreement on this point between the finance minister and myself," Sommer said.
